procedural_history.originating_court: Police Station Mirzapur, District Saharanpur (implied, as the FIR was registered there)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 17.10.2022 passed by the Hon’ble High Court in Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No. 13339 of 2022.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No. 13339 of 2022 in the High Court seeking to quash FIR No. 175 of 2022 dated 11.08.2022. The High Court declined to quash the FIR and dismissed the writ petition, leaving it open for the petitioner to apply for anticipatory bail/bail.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court by way of a Special Leave Petition (converted to Criminal Appeal No. 2344 of 2023) after the High Court refused to quash the FIR. The appellant seeks to have the High Court's order set aside and the FIR quashed.

directions: The impugned order passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad is hereby set aside.
The criminal proceedings arising from FIR No. 175 of 2022 dated 11.08.2022 registered at Police Station Mirzapur, Saharanpur, State of U.P. are hereby quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in declining to quash an FIR where the appellant was not named in the initial FIR, his name surfaced for the first time in a further statement of the first informant, and there were no substantial allegations against him in the entire FIR.

facts: The appellant was not named as an accused in the original First Information Report (FIR).
The appellant's name was added to the case later, based on a "further statement" from the first informant.
The Supreme Court observed that this further statement told an "altogether a different story" than what was narrated in the initial FIR.
There were no substantial allegations against the appellant in the entire FIR.
The Court found that the entire case presented by the first informant appeared to be "concocted and fabricated."
The Court also noted the existence of multiple FIRs, suggesting the case was motivated by a "private or personal grudge" to wreak vengeance.
law: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a High Court has the power to quash an FIR to prevent abuse of the process of law or to secure the ends of justice.
The Supreme Court clarified that the mere fact that an accused's name does not appear in the initial FIR and is added later is not, by itself, a sufficient ground to quash the FIR.
However, an FIR can be quashed if the allegations, on their face, appear to be malicious, concocted, or initiated with an ulterior motive, as per the parameters set in the Bhajan Lal case.
application: The Supreme Court did not base its decision solely on the fact that the appellant was named later. Instead, it considered the totality of the circumstances.

The Court found the credibility of the allegations to be highly doubtful because the informant's further statement, which implicated the appellant, was a significant and contradictory departure from the original FIR.
It concluded that the entire case was likely fabricated and motivated by a personal grudge, as evidenced by the multiple FIRs filed.
The Court determined that the allegations did not prima facie constitute the offenses cited (specifically noting that offenses under Sections 195A and 386 were not made out).
Given that the case appeared to be a malicious prosecution and an abuse of the legal process, the Court found that allowing it to continue would be unjust.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, concluding that it was not justified in declining to quash the FIR. The Supreme Court quashed the FIR against the appellant because the case appeared to be entirely concocted, fabricated, and motivated by a personal grudge, making it an abuse of the process of law.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in declining to quash an FIR where the appellant was not named in the initial FIR, his name surfaced for the first time in a further statement of the first informant, and there were no substantial allegations against him in the entire FIR.
appellant_arguments: The FIR was lodged on false, vexatious, and mischievous allegations.
No offenses are made out against the appellant.
The appellant was not named in the initial FIR.
The appellant's name only surfaced in a further statement from the first informant.
There are no substantial allegations against the appellant in the entire FIR.
respondent_arguments: The FIR should not be quashed because it discloses a cognizable offense.
During the investigation, the complainant's statement was recorded and other material evidence was collected which proved the complainant's claim.

cases.principle: The Court referred to the observations made by the High Court of Patna in this case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any of the provisions of the Code or the concerned Act (under which a criminal proceeding is instituted) to the institution and continuance of the proceedings and/or where there is a specific provision in the Code or the concerned Act, providing efficacious redress for the grievance of the aggrieved party, the proceedings may be quashed.
obiter: It is made clear that we have not adjudicated the contentions raised by learned counsel for the petitioner and the same are left open for the petitioner to raise at an appropriate stage in an appropriate proceeding, in accordance with law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the criminal proceedings against the appellant were an abuse of the legal process, concluding that the case fell within established parameters for quashing an FIR, specifically where the allegations do not disclose an offense, are inherently improbable, and where the proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fides or maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive.
legal_tests_applied: Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same donot disclose the commission of any oﬀ ence and make out a case against the accused.

Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is suﬃ cient ground for proceeding against the accused.

The test for determining whether to quash an FIR in cases of allegedly frivolous or vexatious proceedings requires the court to look beyond the bare averments of the FIR and consider the overall and attending circumstances leading to the registration of the case, including materials collected during the investigation.
policy_considerations: Whenever an accused seeks quashing of the FIR or the criminal proceedings essentially on the ground that such proceedings are manifestly frivolous or vexatious or instituted with the ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance, in such circumstances the Court owes a duty to look into the FIR with care and a little more closely.
It would not be just enough for the Court to look into the averments made in the FIR/complaint alone for the purpose of whether the alleged oﬀence are disclosed or not.

In frivolous or vexatious proceedings, the Court owes a duty to look into many other attending circumstances emerging from the record of the case over and above the averments and, if need be, with due care and circumspection try to read in between the lines.

The Court is empowered to take into account the overall circumstances leading to the initiation/registration of the case as well as the materials collected in the course of investigation to prevent the abuse of the criminal justice system.
